• Не дава́й ему́ сесть тебе́ на ше́ю. - Don't let him take advantage of you.
• Он сиди́т на ше́е у роди́телей. - He is living off his parents.

The full version: сесть на ше́ю и но́жки све́сить - 'to sit on someone's neck and dangle your legs'.

cyr: Flowers in Russia: roses yes, carnations no

examples.ru: Он подарил ей [буке́т] из пяти роз.
examples.en: He gave her a bouquet of five roses.
The veterans were presented with red carnations.

note:
On a first date a Russian man usually brings flowers: a bouquet or a single ро́за.

Гвозди́ки (carnations) are a different story:
• they are taken to cemeteries and monuments
• on May 9 they are given to veterans

The number of flowers matters too: an odd number (three, five, seven) is for the living, an even number for a funeral or a commemoration. So twelve roses is not an ordinary gift.

examples.ru: Первого сентября дети идут в школу с [цвета́ми].
examples.en: On September 1, children go to school with flowers.

note:
The first school day is September 1 and it is called День зна́ний (Knowledge Day).

• children bring flowers to their teachers
• speeches are given at the ceremony in the schoolyard (лине́йка)
• for first-graders, a girl with a bell sits on the shoulder of a graduating senior (выпускни́к) - hence the name Пе́рвый звоно́к (First Bell)

Teachers have their own holiday on October 5, День учи́теля: pupils and parents give them flowers and congratulate them.

related.en: well done; a fine fellow, a hero

note:
Молоде́ц is pronounced «маладе́ц» (an unstressed «о» sounds like «а»).

It means 'well done, good job':
• Ты молоде́ц! - Well done!
• Вы молодцы́! - Good for you all!

It is said to a woman too: Ма́ша, ты молоде́ц! The form does not change, because молоде́ц is in fact a masculine noun (a fine young man, a hero).

cyr: Да нет, наверное: a 'yes' that means 'no'

examples.en: - Are you coming with us? - Nah, probably not.
No, no, everything is fine, don't worry.

note:
In conversation да often does not mean 'yes' but softens the answer.

• Да нет, не на́до. - Oh no, no need.
• Да нет, всё норма́льно. - No, no, everything is fine.
• Да нет, наве́рное. - I don't think so, probably not.

Да нет is a gentle 'no': the speaker hedges and may change their mind.

Conversely, Да ну! expresses disbelief: no way!

cyr: Кто не рискует, тот не пьёт шампанского

examples.ru: Кто не [риску́ет], тот не пьёт шампанского.
examples.en: He who doesn't take risks doesn't drink champagne.

note:
The English 'nothing ventured, nothing gained' has a festive taste in Russian:

• Кто не риску́ет, тот не пьёт шампа́нского.

The saying is used when someone hesitates before a decisive step.

Note the genitive шампа́нского after the negated verb «не пьёт». The accusative шампа́нское is also heard, but the saying usually has the genitive.

examples.en: The guests shouted 'Gorko!' ('Bitter!') and the newlyweds kissed.

note:
At a Russian wedding the guests shout «Го́рько!» ('Bitter!') and the newlyweds must kiss while the guests count the seconds aloud.

The usual explanation is that the drink is 'bitter' and a kiss 'sweetens' it.

• сва́дьба - wedding
• молодожёны - newlyweds
• тамада́ - toastmaster, leads the toasts and the games

A Russian wedding has more talking than dancing: every guest gives a toast.

cyr: The bride ransom: a game at the door

examples.ru: У двери подруги потребовали [вы́куп] с жениха.
examples.en: At the door the bride's friends demanded a ransom from the groom.

note:
The 'ransom of the bride' exists in Russia too, but as a game:
• the bride's friends wait for the жени́х at the door
• they ask questions and set tasks (where is the key, when was the first kiss)
• a wrong answer is paid for with money or sweets

Afterwards the couple go to the ЗА́ГС (the registry office); a church wedding usually comes only after the civil one.

examples.en: The parents greeted the newlyweds with a wedding loaf.

note:
When the newlyweds arrive at the restaurant, the parents greet them with a карава́й: a large round loaf served with salt.

The couple bite off a piece at the same time. Whoever bites off more will, as the belief goes, be the head of the family.

Bread and salt is a traditional welcome for a guest in general: хлеб да соль.

examples.en: The children are watching a cartoon about Cheburashka.

note:
When Russians talk about their childhood, these cartoons often come up:
• «Ну, погоди́!» - a wolf chases a hare
• «Просто́квашино» - дя́дя Фёдор, the cat Матро́скин and the dog Ша́рик
• «Крокоди́л Ге́на и Чебура́шка»
• «Ви́нни-Пух» - the Soviet version of Winnie-the-Pooh

A cartoon is a мультфи́льм, colloquially a му́льтик.

examples.en: On May 9 Russia marks Victory Day.

note:
Russians call the war on the Soviet front the Вели́кая Оте́чественная война́ (1941-1945).

• it began on June 22, 1941, when Germany attacked the USSR
• May 9 is День Побе́ды, the main day of remembrance
• ветера́ны are given flowers, often red carnations

The term does not mean the whole of World War II: for that there is Втора́я мирова́я война́.

cyr: Don't whistle or you'll lose your money

examples.en: Don't whistle in the house, there won't be any money!

note:
Russians do not whistle indoors: a superstition says the money will leave the house.

• Не свисти́, а то де́нег не бу́дет! - Don't whistle, or you'll have no money!
• свисте́ть - to whistle

Similar household habits:
• не здоро́ваться че́рез поро́г - greeting across the threshold brings a quarrel
• присе́сть на доро́жку - before a trip everyone sits down for a moment in silence

cyr: Pull and push: на себя́ and от себя́

examples.ru: Потяни дверь на [себя́], а не от себя.
examples.en: Pull the door toward you, don't push it away.

note:
On doors in Russia you see:
• На себя́ - pull (toward you)
• От себя́ - push (away from you)

The verbs are тяну́ть (to pull) and толка́ть (to push). It is easy to get confused at a store entrance.

Потяни́ дверь на себя́, а не толка́й!

Russian verbs have two sets of present-tense endings.

1st conjugation: зна́ть - зна́ю, зна́ешь, зна́ет, зна́ем, зна́ете, зна́ют
2nd conjugation: говори́ть - говорю́, говори́шь, говори́т, говори́м, говори́те, говоря́т

The 2nd conjugation includes verbs in -ить (except брить, стелить) and some in -еть and -ать: смотре́ть, ви́деть, слы́шать, держа́ть.

All the others (де́лать, чита́ть, рабо́тать) are 1st conjugation.

cyr: Consonant changes in the 1st person: люблю́, хожу́, плачу́

examples.ru: Я каждый день [хожу́] на работу пешком.
examples.en: I walk to work every day.

related.en: to walk, to go on foot

note:
In some 2nd-conjugation verbs a consonant changes only in the 1st person singular:
• люби́ть: люблю́, лю́бишь (б - бл)
• ходи́ть: хожу́, хо́дишь (д - ж)
• плати́ть: плачу́, пла́тишь (т - ч)
• ви́деть: ви́жу, ви́дишь (д - ж)
• лови́ть: ловлю́, ло́вишь (в - вл)

The stress moves too: хожу́, but хо́дишь, хо́дят.

examples.en: A ladybug landed on my palm.

note:
A ladybug is бо́жья коро́вка in Russian, literally 'God's little cow'.

Children let it crawl onto the palm and sing to it to fly away to the sky:
• Бо́жья коро́вка, улети́ на не́бо! - Ladybug, fly away to the sky!

The rhyme has many variants.

cyr: Юрьев день: St George's Day and a saying

examples.ru: Мы купили билеты, а рейс отменили. Вот тебе, бабушка, и [Ю́рьев] день!
examples.en: We bought tickets and the flight was canceled. Well, how about that!

note:
Ю́рьев день is St George's Day. George is Гео́ргий, in everyday speech Ю́рий or Его́р.

A well-known saying comes from it:
• Вот тебе́, ба́бушка, и Ю́рьев день! - Well, how about that: an unexpected disappointment, ruined plans.

Origin: peasants used to be allowed to change their landlord only around St George's Day. When the ruler abolished that right, the saying stayed.

It is said with grumbling, often jokingly.

cyr: Palm Sunday in Russian: Вербное воскресенье

examples.ru: В [Ве́рбное] воскресенье мы пошли в церковь с вербой.
examples.en: On Palm Sunday we went to church with willow branches.
Grandma put some pussy willows in a vase.

note:
Palm Sunday (the Sunday before Easter) is Ве́рбное воскресе́нье in Russian.

In Russia the day is tied to the willow, not to palms or flowers:
• ве́рба - willow, its twigs are taken to church
• ве́рбочки - pussy willows
• Ла́зарева суббо́та - Lazarus Saturday, the day before

After Ве́рбное воскресе́нье comes Страстна́я неде́ля, Holy Week, the last week of Lent.

examples.en: Will you pay cash or by card?

examples.ru: Родители дают мне [карма́нные] деньги раз в неделю.
examples.en: My parents give me pocket money once a week.

related.en: kopeck, a hundredth of a ruble

note:
A копе́йка is a hundredth of a ruble, and it lives on in sayings:
• у меня́ нет ни копе́йки - I don't have a penny
• ни гроша́ за душо́й - the same, a bit old-fashioned
• быть на ме́ли - to be broke

Other words:
• нали́чные - cash: плати́ть нали́чными
• ме́лочь - small change
• карма́нные де́ньги - pocket money

Де́ньги exists only in the plural: у меня́ мно́го де́нег.

cyr: Occupations and women: врач and дире́ктор have no feminine form

examples.en: Our doctor said that everything is fine.
The school principal came to the lesson.

note:
Most Russian occupations are masculine nouns that are used for women too:
• она́ врач, она́ дире́ктор, она́ до́ктор, она́ инжене́р
• the verb agrees with the real sex: врач сказа́ла, дире́ктор пришла́

Some have a feminine form: учи́тельница, певи́ца, актри́са, писа́тельница, поэте́сса.

Forms in -ша (до́кторша) are colloquial and often jokey. Newer forms in -ка (а́вторка, блогерка) are rejected by many.

To stress the sex: же́нщина-врач.

cyr: Хорово́д, сарафа́н and ла́пти: folk dance and dress

examples.ru: На празднике девушки водили [хорово́д] на поляне.
examples.en: On holidays the girls danced a round dance in the meadow.
Grandma put on a sarafan and a headscarf.

related.en: bast shoes, peasant footwear woven from bark

note:
Some words for the old Russian folk life:

• хорово́д - a circle dance with singing; води́ть хорово́д - to dance in a ring
• сарафа́н - a long sleeveless dress, the old women's folk costume
• руба́ха - a long folk shirt
• ла́пти - peasant shoes woven from bast (tree bark), not made of leather

examples.ru: В [роди́тельскую] субботу мы поехали на кладбище.
examples.en: On Memorial Saturday we went to the cemetery.
After the funeral there was a wake at a cafe.

note:
The days of remembering the dead are called роди́тельская суббо́та or помина́ние поко́йных.

• роди́тельская суббо́та - a Saturday when the dead are remembered and cemeteries are visited
• Дми́триевская суббо́та - the Saturday before November 8, St Demetrius' Day
• поми́нки - the memorial meal after a funeral

Flowers are usually taken to the grave.

cyr: Turkic loanwords in Russian: деньги, карандаш, сундук

examples.en: Put the pencil in the pencil case.
Old toys are lying in the chest.

note:
Russian has words of Turkic origin, some of them in very ordinary vocabulary:
• де́ньги - money
• каранда́ш - pencil, literally 'black stone'
• сунду́к - chest, trunk
• база́р - market; colloquially also an uproar: что за база́р?

examples.en: Christ is born! - We glorify Him!

note:
The traditional Christmas greeting and its reply:
• Христо́с рожда́ется! - Сла́вите Его́! (Christ is born! - Glorify Him!)
• or Христо́с роди́лся! - Сла́вим Его́! (Christ has been born! - We glorify Him!)

The reply is 'Glorify Him' or 'We glorify Him', not 'Truly He is born'.

The usual short greeting is «С Рождество́м!», with «с» and the instrumental.

examples.en: For dinner Mom made stuffed cabbage rolls.
Sour cream was served with the cabbage rolls.

note:
• голубцы́ - cabbage leaves stuffed with meat and rice, cooked in a sauce
• долма́ - stuffed grape leaves, from Caucasian cuisine

Голубцы́ have nothing to do with го́лубь, a pigeon: the dish is made of cabbage.

Голубцы́ are usually served with смета́на (sour cream).

examples.ru: В зоопарке мы видели [слони́ху] с детёнышем.
examples.en: At the zoo we saw a female elephant with her calf.

note:
Russian often has a separate word for the female, formed with the suffixes -иц(а) and -их(а).

• лев - льви́ца, волк - волчи́ца
• медве́дь - медве́дица
• слон - слони́ха, ёж - ежи́ха

Some species have one name for both: ко́шка is a cat in general, while ко́т is specifically a tomcat. Лиса́ is a fox of either sex; the male ли́с is rarely heard.

examples.en: Our dog barks at every passer-by.
All night a horse neighed outside the window.

related.en: to neigh; colloquial: to laugh loudly

note:
People hear the same sounds differently in different languages, so the imitations differ.

• соба́ка - «гав-гав» (English 'woof')
• у́тка - «кря-кря» (English 'quack')
• свинья́ - «хрю-хрю» (English 'oink')
• ло́шадь - «иго-го» (English 'neigh')
• коро́ва - «му-у», пету́х - «ку-ка-ре-ку»

Verbs come from them: соба́ка ла́ет, у́тка кря́кает, свинья́ хрю́кает, коро́ва мычи́т, ло́шадь ржёт. Ржать is also colloquial 'to laugh loudly'.

examples.en: This is a really cool movie.
Are you kidding me? I'm serious!

related.en: joke, prank; something funny or odd

note:
Прико́л and прико́льный belong to everyday, mostly younger speech.

• прико́л - a joke, something funny or unusual
• прико́льный - cool, fun, interesting
• прика́лываться - to joke around, to kid someone

«Ты что, прика́лываешься?» means 'Are you kidding me?'.

Прико́л в том, что... means 'the funny thing is that...'.

It sounds informal: fine among friends, not in an official conversation.

cyr: Блин: a pancake and an exclamation

examples.en: Crap, I forgot my keys at home!

note:
Блин is first of all a thin pancake.

But in conversation it is also an exclamation, a mild stand-in for a rude curse. People say it when something surprises, disappoints or annoys them:

• Блин, я опозда́л! - Crap, I'm late!
• Блин, как здесь краси́во! - Wow, it's beautiful here!

It is informal but not vulgar. Better not to say it to an older person or to your boss.

cyr: How to give your opinion in Russian

examples.en: It seems to me that it's cold outside.
I think he needs a rest.

note:
Five common ways to say what you think:

• Я ду́маю, что... - I think that...
• Я счита́ю, что... - I consider that...
• Мне ка́жется, что... - It seems to me that...
• На мой взгляд... - In my view...
• «С мое́й то́чки зре́ния...» - From my point of view...

The clause always starts with что ('that'), preceded by a comma: Я ду́маю, что он прав. English can drop 'that', Russian cannot.

Note: по-мо́ему is written with a hyphen and means 'in my opinion'.

examples.en: I wish you happiness and health!

note:
When «с» and «ч» stand next to each other in a Russian word, they are pronounced together as a long soft «щ».

• счёт - read as «щёт», bill
• сча́стье - «ща́стье», happiness
• счита́ть - «щита́ть», to count
• расчёска - «ращёска», comb
• чересчу́р - «чирищу́р», too much

The same goes for зч and жч: зака́зчик (customer) is read as «зака́щик».

The spelling does not show it: it is written «с» + «ч».

cyr: Желать, дарить, приглашать: verbs of holidays

examples.en: I wish you success in your studies!

examples.ru: Мы [пригласи́ли] всех друзей на Новый год.
examples.en: We invited all our friends to celebrate New Year with us.
Grandma gave me a warm scarf.

note:
Verbs of greeting and gifts have their own patterns.

• жела́ть кому́ чего́ - to wish someone something (the thing wished for is in the genitive): жела́ю вам здоро́вья
• дари́ть кому́ что - to give someone something as a present: дари́ть цветы́
• приглаша́ть кого́ куда́ - to invite someone somewhere: в го́сти
• украша́ть, наряжа́ть что - to decorate: наряжа́ть ёлку

Perfectives: пожела́ть, подари́ть, пригласи́ть, укра́сить, наряди́ть.

cyr: Seeing in the New Year: a Russian saying

examples.en: We always see in the New Year at home.
Where did you celebrate last New Year?

note:
«Как Но́вый год встре́тишь, так его́ и проведёшь» - the way you welcome the New Year is how you will spend it.

So before the holiday Russians:
• finish important work and pay back debts
• forgive offenses
• buy new festive clothes

The verb встреча́ть means 'to meet', and with a holiday also 'to see in, to welcome': встреча́ть Но́вый год.

cyr: The New Year table: оливье and селёдка под шубой

examples.en: Olivier salad is always on the festive table.

examples.ru: К Новому году мы купили килограмм [мандари́нов].
examples.en: For New Year we bought a kilo of tangerines.

note:
New Year is the main family feast in Russia, and the dishes are almost always the same.

• оливье́ - Olivier salad, diced potatoes, vegetables and meat in mayonnaise
• селёдка под шу́бой - a layered salad of herring, potatoes, beets and carrots, literally 'herring under a fur coat'
• бутербро́ды с кра́сной икро́й - sandwiches with red caviar
• мандари́ны и шампа́нское - tangerines and champagne

Икра́ is fish roe: кра́сная икра́ is salmon roe, чёрная икра́ is black caviar.

cyr: Сочельник and колядки: the Russian Christmas Eve

examples.ru: В [соче́льник] многие постятся до первой звезды.
examples.en: On Christmas Eve many people fast until the first star.
Children go from house to house singing carols.

note:
The day before Christmas is the соче́льник, and Christmas (January 7) is Рождество́.

• соче́льник - January 6; by custom nothing is eaten until the first star
• коля́дки - going from house to house singing, for sweets or money
• гада́ние - fortune-telling, especially during Свя́тки (January 7-19)
• Креще́ние - Epiphany, January 19

cyr: Valentine's Day and the Day of Family in Russia

examples.en: She got a valentine from a secret admirer.

examples.ru: [Рома́шка] - символ Дня семьи, любви и верности.
examples.en: The daisy is the symbol of the Day of Family, Love and Fidelity.

related.en: Day of Family, Love and Fidelity

note:
February 14 is День влюблённых (День свято́го Валенти́на) in Russia too, but it is celebrated more modestly.

• валенти́нка - a heart-shaped card
• рома́шка - a daisy, the symbol of the other holiday

The official holiday is July 8: День семьи́, любви́ и ве́рности. It is tied to the saints Пётр and Февро́ния from the city of Му́ром, patrons of marriage.

examples.ru: На Ма́сленицу мы печём [блины́] всю неделю.
examples.en: During Maslenitsa we bake pancakes all week.
Maslenitsa is celebrated before Great Lent.

note:
Ма́сленица is the week before Great Lent, and its main food is блины́. The name comes from ма́сло (butter).

The days have names:
1. Встре́ча - meeting
2. Заигры́ш - the start of the games
3. Ла́комка - the mother-in-law treats her son-in-law
4. Разгуля́й - revelry, jumping over the fire
5. Тёщины вечёрки - the son-in-law treats his mother-in-law
6. Золо́вкины посиде́лки - the young wife treats her husband's sister
7. Прово́ды - the farewell, Прощёное воскресе́нье

The holiday ends with the burning of a straw effigy.

cyr: Не всё коту масленица: a saying

examples.en: Enough partying - the good times don't last forever.

related.en: Maslenitsa, the week of merrymaking before Lent

note:
«Не всё ко́ту ма́сленица» - literally 'it's not always Maslenitsa for the cat': after the fun comes a time of restrictions.

The full saying continues: «..., бу́дет и вели́кий пост» - 'there will be Great Lent too'. Usually only the first part is said.

It is used when someone thinks the good days will last forever, much like 'the good times can't last forever'.

examples.en: God will forgive, and I forgive.

note:
The last Sunday of Maslenitsa is Прощёное воскресе́нье - Forgiveness Sunday. By custom people ask everyone for forgiveness.

1. You say: «Прости́ меня́!» - Forgive me!
2. The reply: «Бог прости́т, и я проща́ю» - God will forgive, and I forgive.
3. Or briefly: «И ты меня́ прости́» - And you forgive me too.

Прости́ is the imperative of прости́ть. The everyday 'sorry' is извини́ or прости́, but on that Sunday the phrase sounds more solemn.

cyr: Verbs with no 'I' form: победить, убедить

examples.en: We will win if we act together.
I will try to persuade him to stay.

note:
Some verbs have no 1st person singular (in the present tense, or in the future for perfectives) because it would sound unnatural.

• победи́ть - ты победи́шь, он победи́т, мы победи́м
• убеди́ть - ты убеди́шь, он убеди́т
• очути́ться - ты очути́шься, он очути́тся

The other forms are normal. For 'I' a workaround is used:
• я смогу́ победи́ть, я хочу́ победи́ть
• я постара́юсь убеди́ть

cyr: Вроде, ведь, вряд ли: three small words

examples.en: He seems to have already gone home.
Don't worry, everything is already done, after all.
He is unlikely to come today.

note:
Three particles that are hard to translate.

• вро́де - 'like' (вро́де тебя́ = someone like you) or 'it seems, apparently'
• ведь - 'after all', 'you know', 'because': it reminds the listener of what they already know, and is often left untranslated
• вряд ли - 'unlikely', 'hardly': strong doubt

Note: after вряд ли the sentence stays affirmative, with no «не»: Вряд ли он придёт - he is unlikely to come.

examples.en: He has been studying the Russian language for five years.

note:
English 'speak Russian' takes a direct object, but the Russian verb of speaking does not.

• знать, изуча́ть, преподава́ть + ру́сский язы́к: я зна́ю ру́сский язы́к - I know Russian
• говори́ть, чита́ть, писа́ть, понима́ть + по-ру́сски or на ру́сском: я говорю́ по-ру́сски

Not: «я говорю́ ру́сский язы́к».

The same goes for other languages: по-англи́йски, по-неме́цки, по-францу́зски.

cyr: Сорок: the odd number 40 and the stress of the tens

examples.en: He is already forty years old.

note:
Among the tens only со́рок is unlike the others: it has nothing to do with четы́ре (four), as English 'forty' has with 'four'. One explanation: it was once a measure of 40 sable skins, enough for one fur coat.

Stress of the tens (often got wrong):
• де́сять, два́дцать, три́дцать, со́рок
• пятьдеся́т, шестьдеся́т - stressed on the ending
• се́мьдесят, во́семьдесят - stressed at the beginning
• девяно́сто

cyr: At the doctor's in Russia: поликлиника, бахилы, регистратура

examples.en: I need to make an appointment with a doctor.
Put on shoe covers before you go in.

note:
A поликли́ника is an outpatient clinic, where a Russian goes with an ordinary illness. Useful words:

• регистрату́ра - the front desk where you book an appointment
• записа́ться к врачу́ - to make an appointment with a doctor
• бахи́лы - disposable shoe covers
• гардеро́б - the coat check
• больни́чный - sick leave: я на больни́чном
• переры́в - a break: обе́денный переры́в

Note that гардеро́б is the coat check, while clothes in general are оде́жда.

cyr: March 8 in Russia: Международный женский день

examples.ru: Он подарил маме [тюльпа́ны] на Восьмое марта.
examples.en: He gave his mom tulips for March 8.

note:
March 8 is a holiday and a day off in Russia. All women are congratulated: mothers, colleagues, friends, grandmothers.

• flowers, most often тюльпа́ны, and small gifts are given
• the working day before the holiday is shorter

Greeting: «Поздравля́ю тебя́ с Восьмы́м ма́рта!»

The date in a greeting is said 'with the eighth of March': the ordinal in the instrumental, the month in the genitive.

cyr: «С лёгким паром!»: a wish after a bath

examples.en: Already washed up? Hope you enjoyed your steam bath!

note:
«С лёгким па́ром!» is said to someone who has just come out of a banya, a bath or a shower; literally 'with light steam'. The English counterpart is something like 'Hope you enjoyed it!'.

It is also the title of the favorite New Year movie «Иро́ния судьбы́, или С лёгким па́ром!» ('The Irony of Fate', 1976), which is shown on TV every year before New Year.

examples.en: We are renting an apartment in the center.
Take off your jacket, it's hot in here.

related.en: to film; to take off; to rent as a tenant
pf.: to film, to take off, to rent

note:
Снима́ть has several senses, and English needs different verbs for them:
• снима́ть фильм - to shoot a movie
• снима́ть пальто́ - to take off a coat
• снима́ть кварти́ру - to rent an apartment (as a tenant)
• снять де́ньги со счёта - to withdraw money from an account

The perfective is снять: сниму́, сни́мешь; снял, сняла́. The owner сдаёт an apartment, and the tenant снима́ет it.

examples.en: Imagine, they transferred us to another office!
Imagine, we won tickets to Paris!

note:
Прики́нь (plural or polite прики́ньте) is slang for 'just imagine', said before a surprising piece of news. It is how friends talk; in a neutral tone say предста́вь(те).

The same verb in its standard meaning is 'to estimate roughly': прики́нуть расхо́ды - to work out the costs roughly.

cyr: Идти, проехать, дойти: motion verbs in figurative senses

examples.en: - Shall we meet at seven? - Deal!
- Sorry, I forgot to call. - It's okay, forget it.

examples.ru: Наконец до меня [дошло́], в чём шутка.

note:
Russian motion verbs have figurative meanings too:
• Идёт! - Deal!
• Тебе́ идёт - it suits you (the person it suits is in the dative)
• Прое́хали - let's forget it (colloquial)
• До меня́ дошло́ - I got it, it dawned on me (colloquial)

cyr: Собаку съесть: to be an expert at something

examples.ru: Спроси Ивана, он на таких задачах собаку [съел].
examples.en: Ask Ivan, he is an old hand at problems like this.
She is an old hand at sales.

note:
The idiom has nothing to do with dogs: на чём-то соба́ку съесть means to be a real expert at something after long practice.

The closest English is 'to know something inside out' or 'to be an old hand at something'.

It is said about someone else or about yourself: Я на э́том соба́ку съел - I'm an old hand at it.

examples.en: Today everything is topsy-turvy for us.
He grabbed the boy by the scruff of the neck.

related.en: scruff, the back of the collar; the nape (colloquial)
inside out, the wrong way round

note:
Шиворот-навыворот means 'topsy-turvy, the wrong way round': де́лать всё ши́ворот-навы́ворот - to do everything wrong.

The first word is ши́ворот, colloquially the back of the collar or the nape of the neck: схвати́ть за ши́ворот - to grab by the scruff of the neck.

cyr: «В Ту́лу со свои́м самова́ром»: carrying coals to Newcastle

examples.ru: Привезти ему яблоки из сада - [в Ту́лу] со своим самоваром.
examples.en: Bringing him apples from the garden is like carrying coals to Newcastle.

examples.ru: Дарить цветы флористу - всё равно что ехать [в Ту́лу] со своим самоваром.
examples.en: Giving flowers to a florist is like carrying coals to Newcastle.

related.en: samovar, a vessel for boiling water for tea
Tula, a city famous for its samovars

note:
Since the 18th century Tula has been known as the city of samovars. The idiom е́хать в Ту́лу со свои́м самова́ром means to bring something to a place where there is plenty of it.

The English equivalent is 'carrying coals to Newcastle'.

It is said when someone's effort or gift is pointless.

cyr: I couldn't care less: мне фиоле́тово and other sayings

examples.en: I don't give a damn what they say about me.

examples.ru: Ему по [бараба́ну], что о нём думают.
examples.en: He doesn't care what people think of him.
I couldn't care less about your grudges.

note:
Russian has many colloquial ways to say 'I couldn't care less'. The indifferent person is in the dative.

• мне фиоле́тово - literally 'it's purple to me'
• мне по бараба́ну - 'it's on the drum to me'
• мне до ла́мпочки - 'it's up to the light bulb to me'
• мне наплева́ть - 'I spit on it'
• мне паралле́льно - 'it's parallel to me'

The neutral ones are мне всё равно́ or мне без ра́зницы - it makes no difference to me.

The colloquial forms are not for your boss or for formal talk.

cyr: The particle же: emphasis that is hard to translate

examples.en: But we agreed to meet at five.

related.en: emphasizing particle: but, after all, you know

note:
The particle же strengthens the word before it. English usually shows it with intonation or with words like 'but', 'after all', 'you know'.

• Ты же обеща́л! - But you promised!
• Ка́кая же ты у́мница! - How smart you are!
• Что же ты молчи́шь? - Well, why are you silent?

It stands after the word it stresses, never at the beginning of a sentence. Without же the same sentence sounds calmer.

cyr: Каша in sayings: not only a dish

examples.ru: Он [завари́л] такую кашу, что все разбираются до сих пор.
examples.en: He made such a mess that everyone is still sorting it out.
In spring the roads are slush underfoot.

related.en: to brew, to pour boiling water over; завари́ть ка́шу - to stir up trouble
to face the consequences: расхлёбывать ка́шу

note:
Ка́ша (porridge) is also an image for a mess in Russian.

• завари́ть ка́шу - to stir up trouble
• расхлёбывать ка́шу - to face the consequences
• ка́ша под нога́ми - slush on the road
• ка́ша во рту́ - mumbled speech

A weak person is told: «Ты что, ка́ши ма́ло е́л?» - didn't you eat enough porridge?

Proverb: «Ка́шу ма́слом не испо́ртишь» - you can't spoil porridge with butter; a good thing can't be too good.

cyr: Riding without a ticket: ехать зайцем

examples.en: He rode without a ticket the whole way.
On the bus I paid the fare by card.

related.en: hare; figuratively a passenger without a ticket

note:
A passenger without a ticket is called a за́яц ('hare'): е́хать за́йцем means to ride without paying.

• безбиле́тник - a fare dodger (the official word)
• контролёр - ticket inspector
• штраф - fine

The fare is called прое́зд: оплати́ть прое́зд. On a bus you will hear: «Оплати́те прое́зд, пожа́луйста» - Please pay the fare.

cyr: New Year greetings: с наступающим and с Новым годом

examples.en: Happy upcoming New Year to you!
We wish you health and happiness!

note:
Russians congratulate in two ways:

• in the days before the holiday: «С наступа́ющим!» (short for «С наступа́ющим Но́вым го́дом!») - Happy upcoming New Year!
• after midnight: «С Но́вым го́дом!» - Happy New Year!

The verb жела́ть takes the genitive: жела́ю тебе́ сча́стья, здоро́вья, успе́ха.

The person is in the dative (тебе́), and what you wish is in the genitive (сча́стья).

examples.en: Every morning he douses himself with cold water.
In winter they swim in an ice hole.

related.en: walrus; also a nickname for a winter swimmer

note:
Зака́ливание is hardening the body with cold, air and water.

• зака́ливаться - to harden oneself
• облива́ться холо́дной водо́й - to douse oneself with cold water
• морже́вание - winter swimming in icy water
• про́рубь - a hole cut in the ice for swimming

Морж is both the animal (walrus) and a nickname for a person who swims in the river in winter.

Зака́ливаться should be gradual, and nobody starts морже́вание without seeing a doctor.

examples.ru: В сказке [ле́ший] заводит путников в чащу.
examples.en: In the tale, a leshy leads travelers deep into the thicket.
The water spirit lives in a deep pool.

related.en: old woman of the forest, in a hut on chicken legs
an evil old man; his death is hidden in a needle
a simple hero who wins in the end

note:
Russian fairy tales have characters you will not know from English-language tales.

• Ба́ба-Яга́ - an old woman of the forest, in a hut on chicken legs
• Коще́й Бессме́ртный - Koschei the Deathless, an evil old man whose death is hidden in a needle
• ле́ший - a forest spirit, and водяно́й - a water spirit
• Ива́н-дура́к - Ivan the Fool, a simple hero who wins in the end
• богаты́рь - a warrior hero, like Илья́ Му́ромец

Дура́к is otherwise a rude word ('fool'), but in a fairy tale Ivan is likable.

examples.en: At the store I bought a bunch of lettuce.

related.en: salad (a dish of several ingredients); also lettuce
Olivier salad (Russian salad with potatoes, eggs and mayonnaise)

note:
Сала́т is masculine: вку́сный сала́т.

It means two things:
• a dish of mixed ingredients with mayonnaise or oil: оливье́
• lettuce as a plant: ли́стья сала́та

A cabbage salad is сала́т из капу́сты, a tomato salad - сала́т из помидо́ров.

cyr: Visiting: идти́ в го́сти and быть в гостя́х

examples.ru: В субботу мы идём в [го́сти] к бабушке.
examples.en: On Saturday we're going to visit Grandma.

examples.ru: Вчера мы весь вечер были в [гостя́х] у друзей.
examples.en: Yesterday we spent the whole evening at our friends' place.

note:
English says 'go visiting' and 'be visiting'. Russian uses two different cases:

• идти́ в го́сти - to go visiting (куда? - accusative pl.)
• быть в гостя́х - to be visiting (где? - prepositional pl.)

The host is «к» + dative with motion and «у» + genitive with being: идти́ в го́сти к друзья́м, быть в гостя́х у друзе́й.

Russians gladly come with a гости́нец, a small gift such as a cake, fruit or sweets, which goes on the table at once.

examples.ru: У нас в доме отключили [горя́чую] воду.
examples.en: The hot water has been turned off in our building.
In summer it's pleasant to swim in warm water.

note:
Hot water from the tap is горя́чая вода́ in Russian. Тёплая means warm or lukewarm.

In Russian cities hot water comes from the city network, so it runs all the time, without a boiler. That is why for 1-3 weeks in summer there is an отключе́ние горя́чей воды́ - yearly maintenance of the network.

• профила́ктика - planned maintenance
• бо́йлер, водонагрева́тель - a device for heating water

On those days people heat water on the stove or use a бо́йлер.

cyr: A warning about «ты»: we haven't drunk to brotherhood

examples.en: Don't address me informally, we don't know each other.

related.en: a toast of brotherhood, a drink to switch to «ты»

note:
If a stranger addresses you as «ты», a Russian may answer sharply:

• Мы с ва́ми детей не крести́ли.
• Мы с ва́ми на брудерша́фт не пи́ли.

Literally: 'we haven't christened children together', 'we haven't drunk to brotherhood'. The meaning: we are not close enough for «ты».

The verbs: ты́кать - to address someone as «ты», вы́кать - as «вы».

The switch to «ты» is agreed on: Дава́йте перейдём на «ты».

cyr: Laughing for no reason: why Russians smile little

examples.ru: Он [улыбну́лся] из вежливости, но разговаривать не стал.
examples.en: He smiled out of politeness but didn't want to talk.
What are you laughing at? Come on, get to work.

note:
A smile in Russia is not automatically a sign of politeness.

• A Russian may answer a stranger's smile with: Мы знако́мы? - Do we know each other?
• Из ве́жливости улыбну́лся sounds cold: the smile was only formal
• At work or in class a smile for no reason looks unserious
• A sincere smile is valued: if a Russian smiles at you, he means it.

There is even a saying: Смех без причи́ны - при́знак дурачи́ны. That is, someone who laughs for no reason is not quite all there.

examples.en: Somebody called you, I don't know who.

examples.ru: Если [кто́-нибудь] позвонит, скажи, что я перезвоню.
examples.en: If anyone calls, tell them I'll call back.
I have something for you (but I'm not saying what).

related.en: someone - I know it happened, I don't know who
anyone, someone or other - not sure it will happen
someone - I know who, but I won't say

note:
Where English has 'someone' and 'anyone', Russian has three forms.

• -то: I know something happened, but not who or what (most often the past)
• -нибудь: anyone at all, unspecified - questions, requests, the future: Позвони́ кому́-нибудь.
• кое-: I know, but I'm not telling: Я кое-что́ зна́ю.

The same goes for что, где, куда, когда: куда́-то, когда́-нибудь, кое-где́.

cyr: Easter in Russia: Па́сха, кули́ч and христо́соваться

examples.en: Grandma bakes a kulich for Easter.

examples.ru: Мы с детьми [кра́сим] яйца к Пасхе.
examples.en: The kids and I are dyeing eggs for Easter.

related.en: Easter; also a sweet dish made of curd cheese

note:
Easter is Па́сха in Russian.

• кули́ч - an Easter cake; every family has its own recipe
• кра́сить я́йца - to dye eggs; red is the traditional color, but any color will do
• сту́каться я́йцами - to tap eggs against each other
• христо́соваться - to exchange the Easter greeting and kiss three times

The greeting: Христо́с воскре́се! - Вои́стину воскре́се! ('Christ is risen!' - 'Truly He is risen!')

Good Friday (Вели́кая пя́тница) and Easter Monday are not days off.

cyr: The last bell: how school ends in Russia

examples.en: The graduates sang songs at the assembly.

examples.ru: Для одиннадцатиклассников [после́дний] звонок прозвенел в мае.
examples.en: For the eleventh-graders the last bell rang in May.

related.en: ceremonial assembly in the school yard

note:
At the end of May Russian schools celebrate the Последний звоно́к.

• лине́йка - a ceremonial assembly in the school yard: speeches, songs, a waltz, balloons
• звоно́к - a first-grader rings a small bell, most often sitting on a graduate's shoulder
• выпускно́й - the graduation party, in June

Where English says 'graduation', Russian separates two things: ЕГЭ is the final exam, and выпускно́й is the celebration.

examples.ru: Говорят, что покупать вещи до родов - плохая [приме́та].
examples.en: They say it's a bad omen to buy things before the birth.

examples.ru: Не хвали раньше времени, а то [сгла́зишь].
examples.en: Don't boast ahead of time, or you'll jinx it.

related.en: superstition, an omen of luck or bad luck

note:
Russians readily believe in приме́ты.

• Before the birth nothing is bought for the baby, and a pregnant woman does not get a haircut
• сгла́зить means to jinx, so people say тьфу-тьфу-тьфу and постуча́ть по де́реву (knock on wood)
• From the роддо́м (maternity hospital) a woman often goes home for a family lunch, usually with just the closest relatives

examples.en: At the store we always buy mineral water.

note:
In a Russian cafe, water with your coffee is usually not free.

• you order and pay for water: во́да с га́зом or без га́за
• во́да из-под кра́на - tap water; many people do not drink it without a filter or boiling
• кипячёная вода - boiled water

The waiter asks: «С га́зом или без га́за?» - Sparkling or still?

cyr: Дед Моро́з: the Russian Father Frost

examples.en: The children are waiting for Ded Moroz and the Snow Maiden.
The presents were lying under the tree.

related.en: the Snow Maiden, Ded Moroz's granddaughter

note:
Дед Моро́з is often called the Russian Santa Claus, but he is a different character.

• tall, with a long beard and a staff, in a long шу́ба (blue, white or red)
• his granddaughter Снегу́рочка (the Snow Maiden) goes with him
• presents are under the fir tree (ёлка), and he comes on New Year's Eve
• he lives in the town of Вели́кий Усты́г

New Year is the main holiday in Russia, and Рождество́ (7 January) is quieter. The greeting: «С Но́вым го́дом!»

cyr: What to bring from Russia: souvenirs

examples.ru: Из Москвы я привезла маме красивую [шкату́лку].
examples.en: From Moscow I brought my mother a beautiful lacquer box.
For the winter he bought himself an ushanka.

related.en: matryoshka, a wooden doll within a doll
Gzhel, blue and white painted ceramics

note:
Classic Russian gifts.

• матрёшка - a wooden doll within a doll
• уша́нка - a winter hat with ear flaps
• плато́к - a shawl; the Pavlovo Posad ones (павлопоса́дские) are the most beautiful
• шкату́лка - a small painted box
• гжель - blue and white ceramics
• пастила́, конфе́ты - sweets (конфе́ты are candies, not confetti)

examples.en: Excuse me, how do I get to the station?
Be so kind, can you tell me what time it is?

related.en: excuse me - the most common way to get someone's attention

note:
Russian has no neutral equivalent of 'sir' and 'madam'.

Суда́рыня and господи́н have gone from everyday speech, and това́рищ and гражда́нка belong to the past. So a stranger is stopped with a formula:
• извини́те
• прости́те
• бу́дьте добры́ - when you are asking for something

The same works for women and men, and the tone decides how polite it sounds.

You also hear де́вушка (young woman) and мужчи́на (man), but some people dislike them, so it is safer to start with извини́те.

cyr: Cheers, bless you, you're welcome: на здоро́вье, за здоро́вье and будь здоро́в

related.en: you're welcome (said when you have served someone food or drink)

note:
English 'to your health', 'bless you' and 'you're welcome' (after a meal) are three different expressions in Russian:

• на здоро́вье - the answer to спаси́бо when you have treated someone
• за здоро́вье - a toast: За твоё здоро́вье!
• будь здоро́в, бу́дьте здоро́вы - when someone sneezes

The trap: на здоро́вье is not a toast, so do not use it to say cheers.

Other toasts are Ва́ше здоро́вье! and Бу́дем здоро́вы!

cyr: Here and there: вот and вон

examples.ru: [Вот] твой ключ, он лежал на столе.
examples.en: Here is your key, it was lying on the table.
Look, there's our train over there!

related.en: over there - far away, you are pointing at it

note:
Russian has two words for pointing:

• вот - here is, there it is; the thing is close: Вот твой ключ - Here's your key
• вон - over there; the thing is far away: Вон авто́бус идёт - There goes the bus

Вот is also a particle of emphasis:
• Вот э́то да! - Well, how about that!
• Вот и всё - That's it.

cyr: Epiphany in Russia: Креще́ние and the ice hole

examples.en: On Epiphany many people swim in an ice hole.
They cut a hole in the ice near the shore.

related.en: a hole cut in the ice for swimming

note:
In Russia Epiphany is usually called Креще́ние, less often Богоявле́ние. The date is 19 January.

The best-known custom is swimming in a про́рубь, a hole in the ice:
1. the person crosses himself
2. plunges in three times
3. this is done in the night of 18-19 January or during the day on the 19th

Priests and doctors warn that it is only for the prepared, and that you should not cut a hole yourself.

People also take свята́я вода́ (holy water) home from church.

cyr: The white crow and the black sheep

examples.ru: В классе он всегда был [бе́лой воро́ной].
examples.en: In class he was always the odd one out.
In the family they considered him the black sheep.

related.en: a person who differs from the others and does not fit in
a member of the group who brings shame on it
a mangy sheep, a member who ruins the group's reputation

note:
Russian has both images, and they are close to English 'odd one out' and 'black sheep', but the emphasis differs.

• бе́лая воро́на - someone who stands out and does not fit the group; not necessarily an insult
• чёрная овца́ - someone who is a disgrace to the family or group; clearly negative

For a bad member of the group Russian more often says парши́вая овца́: парши́вая овца́ всё ста́до по́ртит (one mangy sheep spoils the whole flock).

cyr: These are only flowers, the berries are still to come

examples.ru: Это были только [цвето́чки], а ягодки ещё впереди.
examples.en: That was only the beginning, and the worst is still ahead.

note:
A Russian expression that sounds like summer but has nothing to do with it:

Э́то ещё цвето́чки, а я́годки впереди́.

Literally: 'these are only little flowers, the berries are ahead'. It means that what is happening now is only the beginning and the real trouble comes later.

• цвето́чки - the first, smaller problems
• я́годки - the real, bigger problems

The expression is used for troubles, not for good things.

cyr: Tea in Russia: чай and herbal tea
note:
In Russian, чай without an addition means black or green tea.

• чёрный чай, зелёный чай - ordinary tea
• травяно́й чай - herbal tea, for example with рома́шка (chamomile) or мя́та (mint)
• лека́рственные тра́вы - medicinal herbs; chamomile and mint are more often thought of as these

So in a cafe ask for «чёрный чай» or «зелёный чай».

Tea is usually served with something sweet: пить чай с то́ртом, к ча́ю подаём пече́нье. Чаепи́тие is that whole ritual.

examples.en: I've been looking for a job for a month.

note:
The verb иска́ть has a consonant change in every person, not only in the first:

• я ищу́
• ты и́щешь
• он и́щет
• мы и́щем, вы и́щете
• они́ и́щут

Ск becomes щ. There is no form «я искаю». The past tense is regular: иска́л, иска́ла.

For something specific it takes the accusative: иска́ть рабо́ту. For something abstract it can take the genitive: иска́ть сча́стья.

cyr: A glass in a holder: подстака́нник

examples.en: The conductor brought us tea in a glass holder.

related.en: faceted glass, a glass with flat sides
a metal glass holder with a handle
train car attendant: checks tickets, serves tea and bedding

note:
On a Russian train tea is traditionally served in a special glass.

• гранёный стака́н - a glass with flat faces
• подстака́нник - a metal holder with a handle into which the glass is put
• проводни́к (проводни́ца) - the car attendant: checks tickets, serves tea and bedding

The подстака́нник is often bought as a souvenir today, and for many people a train ride with one is a symbol of a long journey.

cyr: Кварти́рник: a concert in an apartment

examples.ru: В субботу мы идём на [кварти́рник] к друзьям.
examples.en: On Saturday we're going to an apartment concert at some friends' place.

note:
Кварти́рник is an informal concert in someone's apartment: the performer plays or sings in a room or in the kitchen, and the audience sits on chairs and on the floor.

• кварти́ра - an apartment
• кварти́рник - a concert in an apartment

They were popular in the USSR in the 1970s and 1980s and are in fashion again. Russians now organize them outside Russia too.

cyr: Playing cards: suits and court cards

examples.ru: Давай сыграем в карты: [коло́да] у меня есть.
examples.en: Let's play cards, I have a deck.

note:
The Russian names of playing cards are not always what you expect.

• коло́да - a deck
• пи́ки - spades
• тре́фы - clubs
• бу́бны - diamonds
• че́рви - hearts
• туз - ace
• коро́ль, да́ма, вале́т - king, queen, jack

cyr: Disney in Russian: titles of the cartoons

examples.en: Children love Cinderella and Snow White.

note:
Many Russian titles are not literal translations of the English ones.

• Руса́лочка - The Little Mermaid
• Зо́лушка - Cinderella
• Белосне́жка и семь гно́мов - Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs
• Ле́ди и Бродя́га - Lady and the Tramp
• Спя́щая краса́вица - Sleeping Beauty
• Коро́ль лев - The Lion King

Note: for a mermaid Russians say руса́лка, while сире́на is an alarm or a signal.

cyr: To fall in love: влюби́ться and other words

examples.ru: Он [влюби́лся] в неё с первого взгляда.
examples.en: He fell in love with her at first sight.
She has been pining for him for a long time.

note:
To fall in love is влюби́ться, and the action and the state are different:

• я влюби́лась - I fell in love (a moment)
• я влюблена́ - I am in love (a state)

Other words:
• со́хнуть по + dat. - to pine for someone: она́ со́хнет по нему́
• втю́риться в + acc. - colloq., to fall in love, often hard
• потеря́ть го́лову - to lose one's head over love

cyr: Гарри, Гамлет, Голливуд: «г» in place of «h»

examples.en: We watched 'Harry Potter' as a family.

note:
In older loanwords, names that begin with the sound h in the original are written in Russian with the letter г.

• Га́млет, Га́рри - Hamlet, Harry
• Ги́тлер, Га́мбург - Hitler, Hamburg
• Голливу́д, Гава́на - Hollywood, Havana
• Голла́ндия - Holland

Newer words have х: хо́бби, ха́кер, Хью́стон, Хемингу́эй.

cyr: To root for: боле́ть за + accusative

examples.en: We're rooting for the Serbian national team.
He was ill with the flu all week.

related.en: to be ill; to root for; (3rd pers. боли́т) to hurt

note:
The verb боле́ть means 'to be ill', 'to hurt' and 'to root for'.

• боле́ть чем - to be ill: боле́ть гри́ппом (я боле́ю, ты боле́ешь)
• боле́ть за кого́ - to root for someone: боле́ть за сбо́рную
• боли́т - it hurts: боли́т голова́ (3rd person, second conjugation)

A fan is боле́льщик.

So «я боле́ю» on its own means 'I am ill'; 'I'm rooting' needs за + кого́.

cyr: The guest of honor: имени́нник and юбиля́р

examples.en: Today our birthday boy is treating everyone to cake.
The guests congratulated the guest of honor on his sixtieth birthday.

related.en: the person whose birthday it is
the person celebrating a round anniversary

note:
English 'the birthday person' has two Russian names:

• имени́нник - the one whose birthday it is (f. имени́нница)
• юбиля́р - the one celebrating a round year: 50, 60, 70

Имени́ны literally means 'name day', but in conversation it is used for a birthday party.

Russians do not celebrate a 40th birthday, which is a superstition. If they do, they say: «Мне опя́ть три́дцать де́вять» (I'm thirty-nine again).

cyr: Going for shashlik: May Day and the barbecue

examples.ru: В воскресенье мы поедем на [шашлыки́] за город.
examples.en: On Sunday we're driving out of town for a shashlik barbecue.

examples.ru: Отец разжёг [манга́л] и начал жарить мясо.
examples.en: Dad lit the brazier and started grilling the meat.

related.en: shashlik, marinated meat grilled on skewers
a brazier with embers for grilling

note:
A Russian does not go 'for a barbecue' but е́хать на шашлыки́ - always plural, на + accusative.

• шашлы́к - marinated cubes of meat on skewers
• манга́л - a brazier with embers on which the шашлы́к is grilled
• да́ча - a country house, where this often happens

May 1 is now «Пра́здник Весны́ и Труда́» (Spring and Labor Day), and in conversation Первома́й. For many it means a trip to the countryside with шашлыка́ми.

cyr: New words of young people: скуф, нормис, пикми, докс

examples.en: He is such a normie, he doesn't stand out in any way.

related.en: a girl who seeks men's approval

note:
New words of young people, some of them from English (докс, пи́кми, но́рмис):

• докс - finding and publishing someone's personal data on the internet (doxxing)
• скуф - a man over 30 who lets his appearance go and does not exercise
• пи́кми - a girl who tries hard to please men (pick-me)
• но́рмис - an ordinary person with no standout traits (normie)

This is internet slang: young people understand it, and it does not appear in formal texts.

cyr: A recipe in Russian: spoons and pinches

examples.en: Put a pinch of salt into the dough.
Stir in one teaspoon of baking soda.

note:
Measures in Russian recipes are named like this:

• столо́вая ло́жка (ст. л.) - a tablespoon
• ча́йная ло́жка (ч. л.) - a teaspoon
• щепо́тка - a pinch

The verbs are in the infinitive or the imperative: размя́ть ви́лкой, доба́вить, перемеша́ть, замеси́ть те́сто, обжа́рить с двух сторо́н.

When the dough turns golden brown, we say подрумя́нится.

examples.en: They bought the baby a bright rattle.
Put a bib on the child.

related.en: pacifier; also the rubber nipple of a bottle

note:
A few words for baby gear:

• погрему́шка - a rattle
• слюня́вчик - a bib
• со́ска or пусты́шка - a pacifier
• буты́лочка - a feeding bottle

Со́ска means both a pacifier and the rubber nipple of a bottle, while пусты́шка is only a pacifier.

About an adult, со́ска is vulgar, so it is for babies only.

cyr: До сва́дьбы заживёт: comfort for a small injury

examples.en: Don't cry, it'll heal before the wedding.

note:
When a child scrapes or bumps something, a Russian says: «До сва́дьбы заживёт!» - it will heal before the wedding, don't worry.

The verb зажи́ть said of a wound means 'to heal': ра́на зажила́ - the wound has healed.

The saying is also told to adults about a small mishap: «Ничего́, до сва́дьбы заживёт!»

The origin is explained in various ways, but none is certain.

cyr: Comparisons with animals: здоро́в как бык

examples.ru: Мой дед в семьдесят лет [здоро́в] как бык.
examples.en: My grandfather is as healthy as a bull at seventy.

examples.ru: Не обращай внимания, он сегодня [зол] как собака.
examples.en: Don't mind him, he's furious today.

note:
Russian likes short similes: adjective + как + noun.

• дово́лен как слон - very pleased
• зол как соба́ка - furious, angry as a dog
• трусли́в как за́яц - timid as a hare
• наду́лся как индю́к - sulking, puffed up like a turkey
• здоро́в как бык - strong and healthy
• спит как суро́к - sleeps soundly

These expressions usually have the short form of the adjective: здоро́в, зол, дово́лен.

examples.en: He grew up in a communal apartment in St Petersburg.
Every month we pay the utility bills.

note:
The word коммуна́лка has two meanings.

• коммуна́льная кварти́ра - a communal apartment: each family has one room, and the kitchen, bathroom and hallway are shared
• платить за коммуна́лку - to pay the utility bills

Communal apartments appeared after 1917, when large apartments were divided into rooms. People lived in them for decades, and a few still exist today, mostly in St Petersburg.

Utilities are коммуна́льные услу́ги, and a neighbor from such an apartment is a сосе́д по коммуна́лке.

cyr: Noticing something about yourself: ловить себя на том, что

examples.ru: Я часто [ловлю́] себя на том, что говорю сам с собой.
examples.en: I often catch myself talking to myself.

examples.ru: Вчера я [пойма́л] себя на мысли, что скучаю по зиме.
examples.en: Yesterday I caught myself thinking that I miss the winter.

note:
To notice something about yourself, Russian 'catches' you.

• Ловлю́ себя́ на том, что улыба́юсь. - I catch myself smiling.
• Я пойма́л себя́ на мы́сли, что хочу́ домо́й. - I caught myself thinking I want to go home.

The structure is always the same:
1. лови́ть (imperfective) or пойма́ть (perfective)
2. себя́ in the accusative
3. на том, что or на мы́сли, что and a new clause

There is no infinitive: на том takes что and a full clause.

cyr: The threshold: why nothing is passed across it

examples.en: Don't stand on the threshold, come in.
Nothing is passed across the threshold.

note:
In an old Russian belief the threshold (поро́г) is the border between your world and someone else's, and the ancestors live beneath it.

• nothing is passed across the threshold, and people do not shake hands or greet each other across it: it leads to a quarrel
• you do not stand on the threshold: come in or go out

The saying: через поро́г не здоро́вываются, не передаю́т. Many Russians still do so today, though sometimes they joke about it.

cyr: Names in conversation: Ва́ня, Ко́ля, Па́ша

examples.en: Pasha is working from home today.
Kolya promised to call this evening.

note:
In everyday speech Russians use short forms of names, and the full name is for documents and a formal tone.

• Ива́н - Ва́ня
• Никола́й - Ко́ля
• Па́вел - Па́ша
• Константи́н - Ко́стя
• Ви́ктор - Ви́тя
• Влади́мир - Во́ва, Воло́дя
• Вячесла́в - Сла́ва

These are not diminutives for children: grown men are called this way at work and among friends.

cyr: Brand names that became ordinary words

examples.en: Hand me the tape, please, the box has come open.
I need to make a photocopy of my passport.

note:
In Russian some brand names have become the name for all similar things.

• скотч - adhesive tape (and Scotch whisky)
• ксе́рокс - a photocopy: сде́лать ксе́рокс
• па́мперс - any disposable diaper, officially подгу́зник
• джип - any SUV, officially внедоро́жник

A флома́стер is a thin felt-tip pen, a ма́ркер is a thicker one.

cyr: A saying from Taras Bulba: hang in there and you'll be a chief

examples.en: Don't cry, hang in there, Cossack, and you'll be a chief someday!

examples.ru: Он долго [терпе́л] боль и не жаловался.
examples.en: He endured the pain for a long time and did not complain.

note:
Терпи́, каза́к, атама́ном бу́дешь means 'hang in there, Cossack, and you will be a chief'. It is known from Gogol's «Тарас Бульба».

It comforts someone who is having a hard time and reminds them that a big goal sometimes demands putting up with discomfort. Parents often say it to children as a joke, for example before a blood test.

It is close in spirit to 'no pain, no gain'.

examples.en: Tomorrow is a holiday, we're not working.

note:
The main holidays and dates:

• Но́вый год - 1 January
• Рождество́ - 7 January (Orthodox Christmas)
• День защи́тника Оте́чества - 23 February (Defender of the Fatherland Day)
• 8 Ма́рта - Women's Day, when flowers are given
• Пра́здник Весны́ и Труда́ - 1 May (Spring and Labor Day)
• День Побе́ды - 9 May (Victory Day)
• День Росси́и - 12 June (Russia Day)
• День наро́дного еди́нства - 4 November (National Unity Day)

In Russian messages a smile is usually just a bracket, without the colon.

• ) - a smile
• ))) - laughter: the more brackets, the bigger the laugh
• ( - sadness

To an English speaker ")))" may look like a typo. Russians put it in almost every friendly message, and a message without it can seem cold.
